subtopic: BEAUCEVILLE, QUE.-REPORTED DELAY IN DYNAMITING OF ICE IN RIVER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: BEAUCEVILLE, QUE.-REPORTED DELAY IN DYNAMITING OF ICE IN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Associate Minister of National Defence. My question will clearly indicate the national scope and interest in public affairs of our group.
In view of the fact that the Associate Minister of National Defence reported to the house on March 9 that an army report recommended the use of explosives to weaken the ice on the Chaudiere river two or three weeks before the anticipated date of the spring break-up, would the associate minister explain why, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of April 5, the army is only now being sent on this annual dynamiting task

when the waters have already risen five to six feet, and the break-up is imminent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Sevigny (Associate Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: BEAUCEVILLE, QUE.-REPORTED DELAY IN DYNAMITING OF ICE IN RIVER
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his intention to ask this question. It is quite true, as I said on March 9, that action by the Canadian army would follow a request from the provincial authorities.
Subsequent to blasting operations on the Chaudiere river at Beauceville last year it was recommended that preparations for such an operation should be made two or three weeks before the expected date of the ice run. However, it was not until Monday, April 4 that a request for assistance from the provincial government was received by headquarters, Quebec command. A group of army personnel were immediately sent from Valcartier to Beauceville, arriving there on Monday evening. Blasting operations on the river commenced at five o'clock the next morning and by six o'clock the ice was moving slowly.
It is hoped that this prompt action by the army will eliminate the danger of flooding at Beauceville.

subtopic: BEAUCEVILLE, QUE.-REPORTED DELAY IN DYNAMITING OF ICE IN RIVER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since this is the third consecutive spring that the army has been called upon to dynamite the ice of the Chaudiere river at Beauceville, does the associate minister not think the time has come to treat this as a normal operation instead of as a recurrent, last minute emergency?

subtopic: BEAUCEVILLE, QUE.-REPORTED DELAY IN DYNAMITING OF ICE IN RIVER
speechtext: On this particular matter, Mr. Speaker, it is the policy to send the army upon the request of the provincial authorities. To date this policy has been followed.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at ten o'clock last night, I had just completed the few preliminary remarks I had to make on the budget speech for the fiscal year 1960-61.
I shall now deal with certain particular aspects. Like several observers, I was surprised at the enthusiasm shown by some hon. members who support the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), when he brought down his budget. That enthusiasm, indeed, has also surprised the Montreal Gazette correspondent, Mr. Arthur Blakely. Here is what he wrote in the Gazette for April 4, 1960:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

I am sorry if I have offended in this respect, and I will try not to do so again.
(Translation):
I shall nevertheless continue my remarks and say, without, I am sure, being out of order, that the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) was right to call this a do-nothing budget.
I noted in the minister's budget speech the advice he gives and the recommendations he makes to the Canadian people so that the government may succeed in balancing this country's financial position.
It is well known that the government itself has been the largest borrower of modern times in Canada.
Today, the Minister of Finance warns Canadians that they will have to cut down on their spending if they want to make both ends meet. The house will no doubt remember the fairly scathing criticism directed in the house by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm against the governor of the Bank of Canada with regard to his annual report.
In various public statements, Mr. Coyne had asked or advised Canadians to cut down on their spending. He repeated that warning in his annual report, and I shall now quote a few excerpts of the Bank of Canada annual report for 1959 to the Minister of Finance, and more particularly a paragraph appearing on page 9 of the English text.
Mr. Coyne says the following:
We must In the end learn as a nation to live within our means, and exhibit the strength and will to do so. It would, in my view, be the path of realism to move firmly in that direction on a broad front without delay.
Further on he says:
For the purpose of maintaining full employment, economic growth and a rising standard of living, we do not need to stimulate a temporarily high but unsustainable rate of consumer spending by means of more and more consumer credit, or of

capital expenditures on a scale greater than our own capacity and willingness to save out of annual production for that purpose. We would benefit more from greater diversification of our production, which could provide a higher average level of employment and one less exposed to the hazard of sudden changes.
And I shall add one of the last sentences in this chapter of the Bank of Canada report, which may be found on page 10, where Mr. Coyne states:
The adoption of sound and balanced programs for future development, the avoidance of excess in spending and borrowing, and the promotion of a more stable and diversified structure of economic activity, have never been so essential to the continued growth and stability of the Canadian economy.
It seems that last Thursday the Minister of Finance finally decided to agree with the governor of the Bank of Canada and, in his budget speech, to give himself and Canadians at large some advice on the art of saving.
In this regard, I should like to quote a few sentences from the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance, on March 31, 1960, as recorded on page 2672 of Hansard:
We must place emphasis on greater productivity and efficiency rather than on sheer size, on cost control rather than on price increases, on greater saving rather than on excessive consumption.
A little further, he added:
In saying this, I am fully aware of the role of leadership that falls to the federal government. It is the responsibility of the government to try to establish the conditions of financial balance within which the endeavours of others can be carried out successfully. Let me assure hon. members that the government is discharging this responsibility.
A little farther on, the Minister of Finance again referred to the matter of saving when he said:
Saving-voluntary, purposeful, constructive saving-is essential in an economic system dedicated to freedom and progress.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance also announced salary increases for federal civil servants. His statement was hedged with oratorical precautions, as though he wanted to apologize for his failure to grant such adjustments earlier, in spite of pressing demands from civil servants' associations across the country.
Recalling the statement he had made on October 13, 1959, when he explained why he did not want to grant salary increases to federal civil servants, he said, as reported on page 2679 of Hansard of Thursday last:
The decision taken by the government, in the light of its financial position, will not preclude consideration being given to the special position of certain categories of civil servants as the government's financial circumstances permit.

A little farther, he added:
It is now nearly three years since there has been a general increase in civil service salaries. The last general increase was authorized by the present government in July 1957, and made retroactive to May 1, 1957.
With regard to this matter, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a slight correction in order to remove any doubts in the minds of hon. members and of the general public.
When the estimates of the Department of Labour were being considered during the session of 1958, my hon. friend, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) insisted on that matter of salary increases for federal civil servants. It may cause some surprise that the hon. member for Megantic should have something to say on the position of this country's civil servants. It is true that I am not a representative of an Ottawa riding; but it is also true that there are public servants in my own. And even if I only represent a single constituency, I am, like all my hon. friends here, spokesman for the nation as a whole.
Some people in my riding are employed in various post offices, some in the unemployment insurance offices, others in customs offices. Most of them are neither clerks, nor secretaries, nor meteorologists nor veter-inaries, which means that only very few civil servants in our district will benefit from the budget increases. Those Canadians do, however, expect their position to be reconsidered, like the various classes of employees elsewhere. It is obvious that the classes of civil servants in my part of the country are the same or, at least, similar to those in other districts, in cities and towns of similar size. Those people too are entitled to the salaries provided for their jobs and their responsibilities.
I pointed out before, in a quotation, that recruiting needs had guided the minister in his decision.
I know personally that, in our district, some young people who would have all qualifications for certain jobs, positions in the unemployment insurance office, for instance, even refused to submit to the various examinations, because of the insufficient salary provided and also to a certain extent, because of their small prospects of getting higher pay. Such conditions are unfortunate, because the country is thus being deprived of the services of well qualified citizens.
There is another field that the minister failed to deal with and I would like to offer a few remarks about it.
But this state has other servants than those who work in the federal civil service, either internal or external. There are also provincial employees, and employees of municipalities and school boards. I should like to say a word on the latter two classes.
Most mayors and aldermen of cities and towns and councillors of rural municipalities, as well as members of school boards, ordinarily work without remuneration. Some of those devoted public men go to some personal expense, often more than would appear to be either fair or necessary.
This anomaly has been recognized by some municipalities, and in some cases provincial

legislatures have granted them authority to remunerate their elected officials.
The federal government, under statute 1-2 Elizabeth II, chapter 40, entitled: "An act to amend the Income Tax Act", has recognized that fact. And the then Liberal government enacted paragraph 3 of section 10, which I will not read. I have it here, it is a bit long and couched in legal phraseology, the chief merit of which is certainly not clarity.
I am informed that, in many cases, those elected municipal officials cannot benefit from the provisions of the act, because their allowance is not considered as expenses, and that it must be added to their income. It will be agreed that the St. Laurent government took a step in the right direction, and it will be agreed also that after eight years, it is now necessary to take a further step.
In the last eight years, the expenses of mayors and aldermen, and of school trustees, have increased for all kinds of reasons, and it does not seem fair to me that those citizens should be called upon to pay a double tax, that is, both on their income and on the expenses they incur in the fulfilment of their duties.
Must school or municipal boards provide that part of the remuneration shall be considered as a salary and the other part as expenses? On reading over the section I referred to earlier, it seems that this is the case.
However, since it is a matter of income, I do not believe the federal government would be going beyond its jurisdiction if it were at least to investigate the position in which mayors and aldermen of our cities and municipalities, and school trustees, find themselves in this respect.
I believe the government would lose very little in the way of income if a minimum remuneration were made exempt from taxation for these people.
I urge the Minister of Finance to study this aspect of the matter and take corrective action as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I now want to conclude my remarks by talking about confectionery and chocolate manufacturing establishments, and also soft drink bottling plants, in respect of the sales tax. This tax is levied to the extent of 11 per cent, of which 8 per cent goes into general revenue and 3 per cent into the
The Budget-Mr. Roberge old age security fund. It will be recalled that in 1957, the Liberal government had removed the excise tax on soft drinks. The minister has no doubt received the briefs submitted by the association of confectioners and chocolate makers in 1959 and also in 1960. Those briefs are quite explicit and are worthy of consideration.
There have been situations in the past that made such sales taxes necessary, but it does seem that those situations no longer exist and that taxes on chocolate and soft drinks should now be removed.
The brief emphasizes the fact that at least 10,000 people are employed in the chocolate industry with total earnings of over $25 million. A certain number of people are living from the sale and distribution of those products. Research made on the subject definitely shows that sales of those products are reduced as a result of taxation. The tax also cuts down purchases of commodities used in connection with those products, and this in turn prevents any development of national production in that field. There seems to be no doubt that complete removal or at least a material reduction of the tax, would result in increased production.
A proper promotion campaign could boost consumption and therefore create new jobs at both the production and the distribution levels. The general outcome of such action, as far as revenue is concerned, would probably be increased returns from that tax in relation to the number of sales. I think that in this case the old saying: "The sales make the profit", is particularly applicable.
At all events, people employed in that industry would pay income tax since they would hold jobs, and unemployment would be relieved accordingly.
What I have just said about the chocolate industry also applies to the soft drinks industry. I have here a short brief prepared by the manufacturers and I should like to put a few excerpts on the record. I quote:
Removal of the sales tax on soft drinks will enable bottlers to:
(a)	Employ several hundreds additional workers,
(b)	Compete on an adequate basis with tea, coffee, chocolate drinks, canned and non-aerated fruit juices, popsicles, ice cream, soft drink powders, etc.-
(c)	Develop their business and provide many local advantages.
The brief goes on to show that removal of the tax would likely enable 573 bottling plants to supply jobs to 1,600 and even 2,200

The Budget-Mr. Rowe more men, not including salesmen. To complete this quotation, I should like to put on record the last paragraph of this brief:
From 1,600 to 2,100 men will no longer be unemployed and the government will not have to pay unemployment insurance on their behalf. Instead, they will promote the local economy with the money they will spend; they will be paying taxes as well as contributing to unemployment insurance.
Those were the remarks I wanted to make in this house about the third Conservative budget.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must inform him that his time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to deviate for a few moments from the subject now under debate in order to extend the sympathy of, I am sure, everybody in the house to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel), chief whip of the opposition party, in the sad bereavement which he and his family suffered yesterday in the death of Mrs. Habel.
I realize that the annual budget is always an issue of keen national concern. This large budget is no exception, and before dealing with some of the implications may I extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the able presentation he made the other day. It has been my privilege to observe at close range eight different ministers of finance in this parliament, and I may say that I think Canada has been very fortunate in having the outstanding talent, the high type of character, the devotion to duty and the distinguished service given by all these gentlemen. I feel we are still fortunate in having the hon. member for Eglinton as our present Minister of Finance. In native ability, in culture, in devotion to duty and industry I think he is unexcelled by any of his illustrious predecessors.
I know we all have a sense of pride stirred within us when we read that our gross national product has exceeded $35 billion. I must say, however, that as long as we have an unemployment problem and huge deficits on international payments and trade, I think we should beware of taking the size of the gross national product as a sound yardstick of our progress as the former government did. It is true that it indicates the vastness and variety of our resources and the native ability of our people. It is true that it emphasizes that no matter what may lie ahead we as Canadians hold the blue chips in terms of natural resources. We have more resources than any country with a similar number of people has ever enjoyed and we have need


of a farsighted, vigorous, energetic population characteristic of this northern climate.
With respect to those totalitarian people with whom we are forced to compete we must be wary of following the pattern of smug complacency followed by the previous government and of failing to recognize that we are meeting a new form of international competition from another type of society altogether. We have to stop and take stock of the totalitarian dictatorship which now controls half the world. They think they can outdo us, as it were, and gain economic supremacy over us. They believe we have grown soft as a result of our high standard of living and what they regard more or less as our reckless extravagance, short working hours and so forth. They believe we have grown soft and as a result shall fall like ripened fruit into their hands.
I think they underestimate us in holding that view but at the same time I suggest that we must avoid the pride and complacency that seemed to characterize those who ruled this country over a long period of time. We can rejoice in the fact that we have vast resources and a high standard of living but despite this we should at this period in our development tighten our belts a little and go to work in an effort to face the challenge of this problem.
It has been my privilege to watch the progress of this young country for some time both from the fields of agriculture and the factories of industry. I have been privileged by the sufferage of Dufferin-Simcoe to listen to more than one third of all the annual budgets that reported the progress of this dominion in this house and therefore I would feel unworthy of the responsibility that my experience imposes if I hesitated to draw attention to trends that I believe have been and are dangerous to the security and progress of this country. It may be somewhat unpopular to refer to these trends but may I suggest it might be economically disastrous to ignore them.
We must face these issues. We cannot avoid them and we do not desire to. One trend that has been dangerous in my opinion has taken the form of a surrender by all parties to what I might describe as popular or political clamour to have governments do so much for so many. I am not so reactionary as to suggest-indeed, I do not admit that I am reactionary at all, but I do not suggest- that there is not a need for social welfare legislation-I am not unmindful of the fact that while on one hand we talk about our high cost of production and our high cost economy we are, on the other hand, handing out to the people in many cases assistance to

provide things which they should earn for themselves and which falls within individual responsibility to provide. We have a great free enterprise system but it is overburdened with all these costs that must come from the production of that system.
One of the chief reasons why the remnants of the one third great Liberal party are now sitting in the shades of opposition is because approximately one half of our industrial enterprises and three quarters of our raw ore resources are controlled by foreign interests. The people of Canada are anxious to have our economic independence restored before it is too late. That is why we have had the change of government.
With regard to the increasing responsibilities in the field of so-called social welfare, I realize it is probably of little use referring to the value of the dollar in 1925 and the value of the dollar today, but surely it makes us stop and think when we realize that the cost of the welfare aspect to our economy today is more than four times greater than the total cost of all government administration when I first entered this parliament. Surely we should stop and take stock at this stage in our development.
As a consequence of the trend to which I just referred it is probably difficult to reconcile such a highly burdened economy with the economies of other countries with whom we compete in the production of finished goods and where wages are less per day than our costs are per hour.
May I venture to suggest to industry that they must lower their costs to meet this type of competition. That is their chief duty. That is a primary function of business management. Management must devote itself to this daily task in order to survive. The management of Canadian industry today is I believe among the best in the world. It operates with a high standard of employment and maintains the highest wages and shortest working hours and more frequent coffee breaks than business management in any country of the world except the United States, and yet we try to meet the additional burden that confronts us.
It is obvious that industrial management in this country is good or it could not survive under these conditions and pay all the fringe benefits it does and still pay to the government in the form of other charges over 50 per cent of all it makes.
In every branch of our primary industries we have witnessed a revolution in the production of goods with a corresponding reduction in manpower. In agriculture we have witnessed the same thing. We see today that twice as much can be produced as was 79951-0-188
The Budget-Mr. Rowe produced 25 years ago employing one-third as many people. It is estimated that inside of a very few years agricultural production employing only 10 per cent our people will produce more than is produced today.
During this period of transition it is important that we be alert to these changing conditions. When the opposition were in power they seemed almost to have fallen asleep. They ignored these changes which screamed for attention before their very eyes. They did little to provide for employment in other fields of enterprise. They dismally failed to give the necessary encouragement for the establishment of secondary industries and employment therein which industries would process finished products in this country. Indeed, clinging to their old free trade doctrines they encouraged the importation from low wage foreign countries of finished products with a high labour content and apologized for it by expressing the need to buy finished goods everywhere so they could sell our raw products with a low wage content in the markets of the world. It is not difficult to sell goods to someone who wants them or to someone who cannot do without them. This form of economic appeasement has been unsound.
As a result of the policies of the previous administration the expansion of industry and the creation of jobs in Canada was only about half as good as it has been in the same period in West Germany, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States. It is important to remember that three of those countries, as all hon. members know, underwent destruction during the war. Despite that their industries have been rebuilt. They have increased their industrial activity and employed people just twice as fast, percentage-wise, as Canada has.
Do not let us fall into the old Liberal habit of believing in that kind of optimism where you say that everything is fine as long as it does not happen to me. This country is strong and virile. Indeed, it has to be to stand that type of complacency. It has also, to the extent to which I have referred, failed to maintain its place in probably the most active industrial expansion period of the world. Like the lost minute, those days are gone forever. Had we not failed in that period the immigration policy would be different today. We would not be having a curtailment to less than one third of the immigrants we brought in in 1913. We would not have had the situation where 510,000 of our educated boys and girls were going to the United States to find employment in the last five years of the former regime.

The Budget-Mr. Rowe
These things should be studied, Mr. Speaker. There was a time when they should have been taken at the flood. There was a time in world prosperity when we should have been alerted in a business way rather than stay in this smug complacency. The result of it is we find ourselves today with international deficit payments of $1,500 million and a trade deficit of over $500 million, and dividends going out of this country to those who control half our industry and three quarters of our raw resources. At the end of last year it amounted to $500 million. That did not come about because this government was elected; that did not come about overnight; that was established and left, with the consequent growing unemployment, on the doorstep of the present government. For the second time in my years in this house we have had that heritage from the Liberal champions of free trade.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we have a lack of population. My hon. friend is mumbling something but I hope he is thinking more than he is talking. We find that the lack of population is closely associated with the unemployment problem. I am sure that it is recognized by every hon. member within the sound of my voice as the chief problem and as the chief challenge of this government today. What does the opposition suggest as a solution? The only solution I have heard is that of enlarging the free trade pattern which did so much to create the problem itself. The opposition has suggested free trade with the United States. Then, they suggested free trade with the United Kingdom, but they backed away from that one very fast. Now they have gone farther afield and out into the Atlantic and they say, "We want free trade within NATO. We do not know what we are going to do with the inner six; we do not care what happens to the outer seven, but we will take them all, let the chips fall where they may."
This old doctrine of free trade was outmoded 50 years ago. This reckless trend which has been developed and followed under such complacency, the habit of using our gross national product as the only yardstick, disregarding, as they did, trade deficits every year but one in 10 years before this government came to power, measuring prosperity as they have, exporting our raw products as a specialty and importing finished products as a political expediency, has been as unfair to labour as it has been unsound and extravagant to our economy.
For over 30 years I have sat here and listened to vigorous debates on the unemployment problem, only to see it temporarily


relieved from time to time by the grim necessities of wartime. That is not good enough and I do not believe we have to endure it. I think it can be improved and under this dynamic government that we have elected it will be improved. It has become almost chronic.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, may I pay a tribute to my old friend and colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green), for his untiring and capable influence with other countries toward disarmament. I mention it because we all hope and pray that he may be successful and that we shall have a substantial measure of success. Here let us pause and realize that if he is successful, and if we accomplish the goal we are all striving for, there will be a change in the economic picture. We will have to find a place for those who have been toiling in the extravagant and wasteful work of producing the defence equipment that we have all felt was so necessary. These men must be placed somewhere else; we must find some form of employment for them. Owing to our swiftly changing labour conditions, opportunities for increased employment are not going to be found in agriculture or in the production and exportation of other raw products.
May I again emphasize what I believe has been a tragic misapprehension indulged in by many in this house, namely that we must accept finished goods, with a high labour content, from other countries before we can sell our raw products in other countries. I have repeatedly said this in this house. I am speaking about the manufacturing industry because I am interested in the labouring man. I have probably less manufacturing in my riding than many others. I have no personal interest in management, and I am not connected in any other way at the present time with the manufacturing industry, but I am conscious of the fact, as I believe every hon. member is, that that is the only avenue in which we can find employment to absorb the boys and girls we are now educating. They must be employed by the manufacturing enterprises in this country.
I do suggest that so far as having to buy the finished goods from the countries where we sell our raw products is concerned, as everyone knows, while we hold those blue chips in raw resources and the United States is depleting hers we have a market for those products there and in many countries of the world. Does anyone suggest for a moment, in saying that we have to buy the finished products before we can sell our raw products, that a steel plant that buys the raw ore from Labrador or from Steep Rock will go to the textile people in the United States and say,

"We want to get another load of iron ore. How about the Canadian home market? Have you been able to absorb it all? You are selling twice as much as they are producing for themselves. You are getting in on their textiles, but do you think you are getting enough of them?" Does anyone for a moment think that is the situation? No, Mr. Speaker. It might happen in a country under a dictatorship, but it does not happen in those countries where we hope to develop our greatest trade.
Do not let us forget, that the United States and other countries buy raw products from us as and when they need them. If it were otherwise, we might achieve a favourable trade balance. We buy more finished products from the United States than any other country, and this has been true for the last half-century. We have been buying more every year during the last 10 years except one, and that was during the Korean war. If that theory is sound, then why does the United States of America not take our uranium when we want to sell it so badly? Stop and think about it, gentlemen.
I can well recall the days when the Liberal party was in power, and twice in the history of their government the United States closed us out of their market for western cattle and other agricultural products. There was the Fordney-McCumber tariff in the late 1920's and the Hawley-Smoot tariff in 1929. The late Right Hon. Mr. King warned us to be careful not to provoke the United States with any trade proposals because of our raw products going to the United States. We were buying a million dollars worth of products per day more from them than we were selling and yet overnight, Mr. Speaker, as you will recall, they closed their market to our western cattle and agricultural products.
I mention these things to remind this house and to remind the country that we do not need to take the finished products of these foreign countries to the exorbitant extent we are today merely for the sake of selling raw products which have less workmanship content in them. This policy is unfair to labour. It is extravagant and unsound to our economy. Surely, if we learn slowly, we learn by experience that this condition is not as it has been represented.
No, Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that after all when we need markets so badly the only market in the world over which we have any control is our own. It is one of the greatest markets in the world. No similar number of people buy so much in the way of manufactured goods and consumer goods. We buy as many automobiles, frigidaires, 79951-0-1881
The Budget-Mr. Rowe radios and television sets as many countries that have over 100 million people. This is a great potential market that will give increased employment and will do more to solve the problem of markets for agricultural products in the long term than all the parity prices and novel ideas that we have had presented as solutions for agricultural problems. No other development is as necessary as the development of that home market.
The possibilities for development of that market are illustrated by the fact that we are paying about $270 per capita for products from outside the country. Just stop and think of it; that is 10 times per capita more than any other important industrial country in the world ever bought from outside its borders. Should we wonder that we have unemployment, that we have to build post offices, give handouts, enact social legislation and so forth? I have always known that you cannot put much politics into business, but let us try in this time of challenge to put a little business into politics. Let us observe these facts that are screaming for solution. I think the United States of America buys about $28 per capita of products from outside the country.
I am glad to observe that our government has taken into account the difficult conditions in the textile and other manufacturing industries. I am glad they are taking a step in the right direction in that regard. I am glad to observe that they are trying to get away from that free trade pattern that was set by their predecessors. This is a change for which the people of Canada voted; this is a change which the people of Canada expect from this government, led by a dynamic Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), who is supported by one of the ablest cabinets we have had in Canada since confederation. This government has more numbers behind them, and more youth and clean-cut ability than I have experienced in my time. This is a great opportunity to put into effect the policies for which this party stands, the traditional policies for the development of our own resources within our own country. I am sure that is what this government is trying to do. Despite the handicaps that manufacturing industry has had, the high taxes, stubborn competition, they certainly employ more people, pay more of our taxes and give needed freight tonnage and freight revenues to our railways to a greater extent than all the other industries of Canada combined except mining.
I can only suggest that it is rather amusing to me that those who are struggling to hold together the tattered remnants of the Liberal party, are feebly drawing attention to the related problems of unemployment. You

The Budget-Mr. Rowe would imagine this problem had only developed since the election. It has been said that Rome was not built in a day. These issues have not developed overnight. We find that unemployment has been almost chronic for some time in this country. They tell us now that the unemployment situation is bad and that our per capita debt is terrible. You would think these conditions only arrived overnight. They do not tell you that the debt more than doubled in the last five years of their regime. They say the international balance of payments situation is bad, but they do not tell you that during the last five years of their government our deficit in goods and services totalled over $6 billion. This heritage has again been dropped on the doorstep of the incoming government.
These are some of the reasons the opposition gives for having no confidence in the present government. May I suggest it is very amusing because it just emphasizes why the public has not any confidence in them. In the interest of enlarging our home market for farm products, employment for an increasing population and strenghtening our national economy, I urge the government to restore confidence and stability in our manufacturing industries. Changes must be made in that old free trade pattern that has already threatened our economic independence. Had it not been for the extravagant stimulus of defence production, this dangerous trend would have been far more conspicuous.
The manufacturing industry is indigenous to a sound economy. Its encouragement and expansion are now as equally challenging to the government as are the agricultural problems. These two industries are complementary and neither needs to be sacrificed in the interest of the other. The employment in the factories of industry is as vital to this country as the work in the fields of agriculture.
I say again, and this may be politically unpopular, that it is economically dangerous to avoid this problem. The future of our industrial growth is unlikely to be confined to either the St. Lawrence or great lakes areas. Indeed, Winnipeg now challenges the record of Hamilton, as we see the smokestacks rising in the wheat fields of Saskatchewan. Edmonton and Calgary seem to hold happy arguments as to their greatness in their rich and lucky province. Indeed, the hope of the maritime provinces as well as the great prosperity of British Columbia depends on the steady growth to which I have referred. We are facing a new age in these swiftly changing times in a world that is becoming industrialized more rapidly all the time.

I do not believe our customs and tariff structures in this country have changed much in 50 years. I think it is high time that we streamlined and modernized our approach to these gigantic problems as we face days of possible economic adversity such as we have never experienced previously. As you know, Mr. Speaker, our tariff structure has been kicked around all during these years as a political football. I have had a couple of passes at it myself. It has been nicknamed to suit the season and to suit the occasion. It has been called "reciprocity" sometimes. At others it has been called in debate "brick for brick", "don't provoke the U.S.". At other times it has been called a "counter-vailling duty plan". Sometimes the policies have been fixed more in Washington than in Ottawa. It is about time that we took a straight or new look and did a little bit of a face-lifting job on our whole customs and tariff structure which has not had an investigation since 1907. I think we must modernize and streamline this approach.
In this regard may I suggest and urge upon the government the necessity of giving consideration to the enlargement of our tariff board so that it might give hearings to direct appeals and submissions from producer and consumer organizations that might expedite its findings and recommendations accordingly to the government.
Before closing may I again mention the general agreement on tariffs and trade, commonly known as GATT. This is another child of the former government left, for better or worse, on the doorstep of the present government. We were told by the former government that before they went over to negotiate this treaty, "we lowered our tariffs more than anybody else before we entered negotiations, and that is why they liked us so much". They made the agreement. Strange as it may seem, the present government has adhered to it more diligently probably than many of the other signatories. However, if our industrial employment is going to be unduly endangered by adherence to GATT, I think we had better consider the advisability of having a more practical fiscal policy made in Ottawa rather than in Geneva. Even in these days of such great international tension and uncertainty we cannot afford to sacrifice our economic independence on the altar of world diplomacy.
In closing I wish to pay a compliment to our dynamic Prime Minister for his efforts, during election time and since then, to bring to this great young country of Canada a greater degree of national unity. In that regard I believe we can all say that this government has succeeded to no small degree. In our provincial and dominion relations, and

in all classes, races and creeds are more closely united than they have ever been at any time since I entered parliament. I believe a great deal of credit is due to this vigorous new government in Ottawa. Despite these challenges and despite our troubles the future is not as dark as some might think it to be. I believe it will be a brighter future if our people are encouraged to face realities. I believe we need that same type of unity that marked the habits and practices of our people in this country when our survival was at stake, at that time their achievements surprised the world. I believe that type of unity between the west and the east, the farmer and the manufacturer, industry and labour, the capitalist and the shareholder, and between provincial and dominion governments must be re-established. Our people will then guarantee a sound economic future that can maintain a way of life that no other people have ever approached.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I shall like to associate myself and the C.C.F. party with the opening remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (M. Rowe) in which he expressed the great sorrow of all of us on learning of the passing of the wife of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel), the Liberal chief whip. To our colleague and to the family we extend our utmost sympathy at this time in their bereavement.
It was like old times, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. He has played a distinguished part in the public life of this country for many years. Sitting now on the government side of the house he has shown today something of the old fire and talent in debate that we have had displayed so often in the house. As a friend for some considerable length of time I want to tell him sincerely that I hope he will in the future avail himself of the opportunity to speak more frequently than he has in the recent past. I am sure he would receive the same kind of attentive hearing he was given this afternoon.
The hon. member started out by pointing out some of the great issues facing the people of this country. No one could have pointed them out more ably than did the hon. gentleman. As a matter of fact, during his opening remarks I was wondering whether he thought he was still on this side of the house because he was pointing out the great deficit in international payments that faces this country, the greatest deficit in history. He was pointing out the tremendous amount of unemployment in this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He was pointing out the tremendous amount of unemployment in this country that has not yet ben dealt with. He went on further to say that these were at least two of the problems that is was necessary for our country to solve, particularly in view of the great challenge to this nation and to other nations in the western world from Soviet competition at this time. However, when the hon. gentleman came to his solutions I think he showed that the Conservative party, particularly if it should follow his advice, is not likely to deal-certainly not in a satisfactory manner-with these great problems that face our country today.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) made a very basic decision many months ago and that was that no matter what happened as far as other questions are concerned, no matter what the degree of unemployment in the country, no matter what the condition of the agricultural industry and no matter what the position of the old age pensioners, the budget would be balanced with as little increase as possible in expenditures. That purpose the Minister of Finance has accomplished and he seems to be highly satisfied with the state of affairs in our country today. In his budget speech, amongst other things, he said this as reported at page 2669 of Hansard:
Twelve months ago when I introduced the last budget we were emerging from a recession.
As reported on the next page he went on to say this:
Last year we emerged from a recession-
As far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, he feels that we are out of the recession and that everything is going well He went on to say this:
We can look forward optimistically to another year of solid expansion and balanced growth.
I do not agree that we have had a year of solid expansion. 1 do not agree that we have had a year of the kind of balanced growth that should commend itself to the minister. I think we have witnessed a year just ended in which Canadians were not doing as well, either by way of production or by way of consumption, as they are capable of doing. There are many great problems facing our nation at this time. These problems have not been dealt with and have not been solved. The Minister of Finance was frank enough to point out that there are more unemployed today than there were a year ago. There are 18,000 more persons out of work and looking for jobs than a year ago. The latest figure

The Budget-Mr. Argue is 555,000; a year ago it was 537,000. Yet the minister is prepared by his statements in the budget to allow this situation to continue. He is making a forecast of the same type of general increase in the gross national product for the coming year as he made in the past year. And very obviously the government has decided that it is going to live with unemployment and it is perfectly prepared to allow unemployment to continue at its very high level.
The government has not brought forward a policy to deal with farm income. The government is reverting to the open market system. It is pulling the props out from under the supports for many agricultural products. It is using the technique of deficiency payments. It announced the other day a small payment by way of deficiency payment on one grade of eggs, and still the producers who brought to market eggs of other grades will receive no payment whatsoever. In the meantime they have lost the benefit of the support for purchase prices that helped maintain a somewhat higher price for those other grades.
The government announced a few weeks ago-I was not in the house at the time; had I been I would not under the rules of the house have had an opportunity to make any comment at that time-that it was saying "No" to the western agricultural delegation. This came as a very distinct shock and great disappointment to the producers of western Canada who had placed so much faith in this government. They had come to Ottawa asking the government to fulfil its promise of providing parity prices. They had asked the government to consider the price-cost squeeze. They had asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to go at least part way toward fulfilling his promise of providing deficiency payments.
But what have they received? I think they received very bad treatment from the Prime Minister. I think they received rather insulting treatment when they had to wait for almost a full calendar year before the Prime Minister finally made up his mind, although ostensibly he was considering it all this time, and said "No, there is nothing for you". We are hoping that this does not close the door for the duration of this parliament on the very important and well documented case of western producers for some assistance. The budget was a disappointment in that no mention was made of any improvement of the position of our agricultural producers.
So there is widespread unemployment. The agricultural industry is being placed more


and more at the mercy of the open, unregulated market against which organized agriculture has complained for so many years. We have seen in 1959 Canada's net indebtedness on international payments reach the highest figure in Canadian history. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) pointed out this afternoon, very properly, that this means our country is in hock to this extent to foreign investors, mainly investors to the United States, and that to the extent signified by these figures our industry is coming more and more under the control and domination of United States capital. The hon. member went on to point out that it was not just a case of an adverse balance of payments on merchandise trade, but that to the extent of $600 million or more we had to pay out obligations as a result of investment of outside capital in Canadian industry.
This raises once more the whole question of our independent control and management of our own industries. How often did government members when they were on this side of the house point out the great dangers that flow from an excessive control of Canadian industries by outside capital? Here, then, is the third great problem facing the Canadian people at this time and about which this budget said little except to accept, in the words of the Minister of Finance, this inflow of capital; and he went on to say that in his opinion it was in the best interests of this country.
There are other problems facing our nation, and I think these problems must be solved in the interest of a higher standard of living for Canadians as well as in the interest of greater control of our industry by Canadians.
The other problem I refer to is the growing number of legalized rackets in the country that result in an exorbitant cost of living for Canadian consumers. I have made some study of the drug industry and I think there is ample evidence to show that Canadians today are paying exorbitant prices in this country for drugs. Canadians' health needs for drugs are being exploited, and I suggest this is a field in which this government and other governments should take immediate and appropriate action.
I have a number of examples of cases where prices charged for certain drugs are, I think exorbitant. The publication "Gilbert Surgical News" of Toronto lists the cost of terramycin hydrochloric capsules at 100 for $42.08, whereas sold under the generic name of oxytetracycline hydrochloric the price for 100 capsules is $28. Similarly, with the brand name Pen-Vee tablets 100 are sold for $50.62,

and under the generic name of phenoxymethyl penicillin 100 are sold for $18. It has been reported that in the city of Toronto hydrocortisone acetate tablets in the 20 milligram size are laid down at a cost of $40 per thousand. Under the brand name of Hydro-cortune acetate they retail at $295 per thousand. It is reported that Largactil, the brand name for a drug known as chlorpromazine hydrochloride in the 25 milligram tablet which is laid down in Toronto at a cost of $2.75 per thousand, is being retailed at $80 per thousand, almost a 3,000 per cent markup.
Here is an instance where appropriate action should be taken, action which would result not only in preventing inflation to some extent but also in rolling back the cost of drugs, a very important item in the budgets of a great many Canadians. I have advocated the placing of this whole question before a committee of this house for study and investigation. Although I am a member of a movement which is very much in favour of public ownership and public development, we are not advocating public ownership for the sake of public ownership. However, the production of drugs is one field where a crown corporation producing essential drugs -not gobbling up the market; not establishing itself as a monopoly, but setting itself up as a pilot production plant-could be very instrumental in controlling the price of drugs.

speechtext:
I am prepared to answer the hon. member's questions when I sit down, but my time is limited.
I think there are many examples of exceedingly efficient public enterprises. I might mention, for example, the Polymer Corporation, which in another field has done much
The Budget-Mr. Argue to keep down the price of rubber. I am not suggesting wide-open public ownership in this area, but I am suggesting that now is the time when parliament should take action in the interest of the health and welfare of Canadians.
There are other rackets in which prices are charged which are altogether exorbitant. In addition to an inquiry into the drug industry I should like to see an inquiry undertaken into the cost of the basic material used in the production of dental plates. There was a report of the combines investigation commission in 1947 which showed that the manufacturing cost of a set of blanks at that time was 15 cents, while the cost to the dentist was $4. Here is another case where there should be a public inquiry.
There is another racket which is widespread in this country to which the government has closed its eyes, and that is the racket in interest rates. Small loan companies, moneylenders, those who provide money for second and third mortgages, are charging interest rates of 15 per cent, 20 per cent, 25 per cent, 30 per cent or more. Here is a whole area in which action should be taken to reduce the cost to consumers of essential goods, thereby reducing the general cost of living and, perhaps, even resulting in a general reduction in the price level in this country.
I feel that the budget should be a plan that it should set forth the government's program to increase production, to increase the welfare of Canadians. I have pointed out some of the problems. I want to make it abundantly clear that in approaching these problems we feel solutions should be found in an atmosphere of the fullest freedom and public discussion. Freedom in this country is not just a question of maintaining parliamentary democracy, though that is essential. It is also a matter of making certain that we have a free press and freedom of discussion; freedom for the dissemination of information.
We feel that in so far as it can be avoided we should resist any growing monopoly in the field of mass media; the field of newspapers, radio and television. Royal commissions have studied this important question in the past. Recommendations have been made that outlets in this field should be separated and independent as far as possible. I believe that the growing concentration of newspapers in Canada has now reached a point which would indicate the desirability of a parliamentary committee inquiring into the degree to which this concentration exists, the rate at which it is being accelerated and to what extent this process impairs the free
2972	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Argue and frank reporting and discussion of public questions. That is why I have on the order paper a resolution asking that a parliamentary committee be set up to look into this whole matter. We are disturbed about the situation which is arising in this country. We are disturbed by what we feel is a potential threat to freedom of discussion in our nation.
We know that the board of broadcast governors decided the other day to recommend the award of a television outlet in Toronto to the Telegram, a newspaper in that city. We question the desirability of newspapers owning or controlling television outlets. We question this development, and we say, along with the royal commission, that whenever possible it is better to have independent outlets and that as far as possible there should be a separation of control as between newspapers, television and radio.
We are looking to the day when there can be a much more rapid development of the Canadian economy. We wish the government would take action as proposed in our subamendment to encourage the accumulation and investment of Canadian capital in Canadian industry, and we think that in all the actions taken by the government everything should be done to protect our resources in the interest of our country. I have been reading in recent days some of the documents which were presented before the energy board, some of the evidence which was provided in connection with the applications for the export of natural gas from our country. I have noticed that with the minister's announcement the government is making provision for the export of vast quantities of Canadian natural gas to United States markets over a period of 25 years at varying prices to a number of companies. We feel strongly that Canadian resources should be developed in the interests of Canadians.
We participated in the pipe line debate in this house in which the government of the day was accused of providing from the substance of this country the material and resources that would result in creating new millionaires and in a greater control of Canadian resources by Texas buccaneers. We have been exceedingly disappointed in that this government since it took office has done nothing to ensure that the resources of Canada are developed more in the interests of Canadians and that no action has been taken to ensure that no more millionaires will be created and that there will be a reduction in the control of these resources outside our nation.


I anticipate much discussion this session of the award made involving the export of gas to these various companies. The people of British Columbia have a particular complaint in that they are being charged a higher rate for Canadian gas than is being paid by United States citizens. I am not satisfied that the energy board obtained the best price for this gas. There seems to be much evidence that the United States market is so large and the demand by United States consumers so high that a higher price could have been obtained for our natural gas. The gas in the southern part of Alberta should to a greater extent be used for Canadians. Since it is our gas it should be Canadians and not the people of the United States who should pay the lower price for bringing gas from the more northerly part of Canada.
There is no indication that I can see that the government through approving the recommendations of the board has not approved everything it comdemned when in opposition. It has gone along with the trans-Canada pipe lines setup. The export of gas is being provided for that company. Even with the development of the export of Alberta gas to California, United States interests are obviously in control of this great operation to the extent, we are convinced, that Canadians are getting less than they deserve from this natural resource.
The figures placed before the board by the government estimate that for the first year of operation Pacific Gas Transmission Company will make a net return on its investment of 12.6 per cent. The Alberta Natural Gas Company will make a net return on its share capital of 14.5 per cent. These are high profits. There is little by way of risk. The market is there and all that has to be done to assure a large profit is to provide marketing facilities.
The whole question of leverage was gone into. In the days ahead I believe it will be seen that this government like the former one has played an undesirable role in making new millionaires and in providing additional millions to present millionaires. It has continued to allow the exploitation of our natural resources without giving the necessary consideration to the welfare of the Canadian people whose property these natural resources happens to be.
As the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has said, our society faces a great challenge today. Many Canadians are disappointed in the budget. I am certain that unemployed Canadians are disappointed that the government has no program to remove unemployment. I am certain that the agricultural producers who look to this government for

help are disappointed. I am certain that some hon. members of the Conservative party are disappointed. The hon. member for Duf-ferin-Simcoe is disappointed that unemployment remains at a high level. I think there are some in the world who are probably pleased with the budget. I would think the occupants of the Kremlin must look with satisfaction at the fact that Canada has unemployment, regional poverty, and that racketeers in the country are exploiting the welfare of ordinary Canadians. They will be pleased that Canada which as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said is endowed with more natural resources for its population than any other nation in the world is just limping along. We will have to do something about these problems not only in the interest of Canadians but in the interest of maintaining Canadian freedom and maintaining Canada as a leader among middle powers.
I am not prepared to admit we cannot solve the great problems that face us but the government does not know the problems exist. The Minister of Finance has closed his eyes to them. He has talked about a balanced growth and has forecast for the coming year the same increase in the gross national product he referred to in the last budget. All these great problems are going unsolved and apparently the government is happy that they are not being solved.
There are a number of principles which should govern our action as a nation in the days ahead. First, we should not be satisfied with our degree of freedom but should increase it. This government should be concerned, as it has not been, with the abrogation of freedom in Newfoundland. The government failed to raise its voice with respect to racial discrimination in South Africa and has side-stepped the issue when questions have been raised on orders of the day. Humans in that nation were whipped to work just as they were on this continent many years ago under slavery and yet the voice of Canada is soft when it comes to this world issue. We should speak out firmly for the protection and preservation of freedom in Canada and anywhere in the world where it is threatened. If we want to have respect in the councils of the nations we cannot have one standard for nations in the commonwealth and another standard for those outside the commonwealth.
The second principle is that as a nation we should invest more in our resources so we can develop them in the interest of the nation. The third principle is that we should embark on a full employment program in Canada, with greater production, and we should
The Budget-Mr. Argue not have the smug satisfaction of the Minister of Finance who shuts his eyes to the suffering of half a million Canadians out of work.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that action should be taken to increase efficiency, to reduce prices, to eliminate waste. One of the places to start is here. We should eliminate excessive prices of essential commodities in our country.
Fifth, I am suggesting that we take appropriate action within our constitution to provide educational opportunities for every Canadian, irrespective of the pocket book of the individual wanting that education, or the parents of our young people looking for an education.
Sixth, contrary to the view of the government that now is the time to hold on, that now is the time to resist any extension of welfare services, I suggest that now is the time to embark on a program of old age pensions for retired persons in Canada which will maintain a pension in keeping with the great productive wealth of our nation. In other words, now is the time to increase old age pensions and social security benefits. I suggest that now is the time for an increase in the health benefits available to Canadians.
Why should Canadians who are sick and need medical attention have to face the tremendous cost of that medical attention? We have a hospitalization program. It is a good program. It will soon be available in every part of Canada. Let us not be satisfied. Let us increase the program. Instead of it being a net liability to Canadians, which apparently is the view of the government, it would be a tremendous asset to our nation to have a program that would remove the fear of heavy medical expenses in time of ill health.
The seventh principle I advance is that we must do everything we can at all times to maintain the integrity and the independence of the Canadian nation. I am not against the people who live in any other country. I feel that citizens of the United States, of the United Kingdom or of other countries in the world have within their jurisdiction the development of the resources of their own nation. We should have the same jurisdiction in Canada. I submit that if we adopt the kind of principles I have put forward we shall improve our standard of living, we shall improve our democratic machinery, we shall improve life in our nation and, above all, we shall make certain that this great development of Canada is for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member for Assiniboia would answer a few questions? One of the things we have to consider and one of the things we have

The Budget-Mr. Argue to be very careful about is that we do not set back the manufacturing of and the bringing out of those new drugs. One of the things that I want to say to him is that about 80 per cent of all drugs-

I have a question I was leading up to. Eighty per cent of all new drugs used today were produced in the last 20 years. The hon. member talked about the cost of prescriptions. One third of the prescriptions issued cost from $1 to $1.99. I ask the hon. member where the high cost comes in there? And only 7 per cent are for $5 and over.
I ask the hon. gentleman another question. He spoke about an investigation into this. Is he going to stop the import of those drugs from Japan and from those other countries that buy the raw material and do no research whatever in the production of new drugs? In other words, would he be instrumental in denying the tremendous cures that we have had in the last 20 years through the production of those new drugs simply because the firms have been allowed a little profit which they can plow back into research?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his important questions. I would not wish to do anything that would stop the development of new drugs.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what the hon. member is suggesting.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would think the development of new drugs is not so much the result of the fabulous profits that are made by some of these drug manufacturing companies but in the main is the result of the company having put together a very large and talented research team, and a research department where people in the main are working on salaries. It is through their research department that they have developed their new drugs. They have not been developed because of the profit motive.
Of course, I would do nothing to discourage drugs coming into our country, needed drugs that have been developed in other nations. I would encourage those drugs being brought into our country by encouraging a lower price that people can afford to pay. I am not talking about reasonable profits. I said I felt there should be some public development; that the production of some of those drugs should be carried on as a pilot operation, not to control the market. If the manufacture of those drugs, in proportion of the instances, was done at a low price I believe the manufacturers would control

some of these mark-ups. I do not think my hon. friend would agree that a mark-up of 3,000 per cent is quite necessary.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my words of sympathy to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) upon the loss of his wife. I think all hon. members of parliament, irrespective of which side of the house they sit on, realize that the whole foundation of our society rests in the home and that the loss of the wife breaks up the home and disrupts the individual. I know I speak for all backbenchers in that regard.
I am also very happy to follow the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). We backbenchers, we newcomers to the House of Commons, feel that the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe is a sort of father of this party, one of the elder members. We remember him in our early days. He used to come out to speak in Saskatchewan and Alberta on behalf of the party. When he speaks we all look to him for wisdom.
I am also very happy to follow the hon. member for Assiniboia, the house leader of the C.C.F., because I may say to him personally that we graduated from the same university. I remember him in those days when we used to debate together. I did not think or realize at that time at the university that he was a socialist. I doubt that very much today.
