subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will not answer that now.
My first words are words of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I cannot help but believe that all hon. members, irrespective of where they sit, appreciate and will accept the premise that the personal prestige and stock of the Minister of Finance are greater and have surely increased since his call to the all-important position of Minister of Finance. He has piloted this country through an economic recession which this government inherited in 1957. On budget night he was able to prophesy a surplus for the coming year. I think great credit is due the Minister of Finance for his policies, recommended to the government, which enabled him to bring in a budget in 1960 which indicates that there will be a surplus next year.
It is always most astonishing for me, as a backbencher, to listen to the inconsistencies

of the members of the opposition. We had some good examples of them today. This is the type of inconsistency that bothers me as a backbencher. Some days the hon. member for Assiniboia gets up and says that this government is financing on a deficit, and is this not terrible? This will lead to nothing but bankruptcy. Then on another day when he is speaking on estimates or some other subject he says, spend more money for the farmers; more money for the pensioners; more money for this and that. This is the type of inconsistency that is very difficult to follow so far as the opposition is concerned.
It can still be balanced at a higher level.

After all, when we took office we inherited a recession in this country and through the efforts of this government, the spending of $1 billion on housing, the increasing of subventions for the coal industry, pouring more money into the unemployment insurance fund, we were able to bring the economy of Canada into a state where we can now see we are moving out of recession and into prosperity. For example, we have spent millions of dollars on a farm support program.
I should like to come now to inconsistencies that are exhibited by an opposition group that does not now sit in this House of Commons- they used to sit here-and I refer to the Social Credit group. Many of the members of that group who sat in this house are now members of the legislature at Edmonton. As this house knows, the Social Credit party has the largest majority in the legislature at Edmonton in the history of Alberta. If they were to criticize themselves, therefore, they would destroy their own house. They have taken on a new function in the province of Alberta and that is the criticism of federal policies. I do not believe any Conservative member of parliament would be disturbed about people going to the polls and defeating him on the basis of principles for which he stood. I am sure he would accept that defeat with good grace. However, I would hate to be a candidate in the constituency of Bow River and realize that I had been defeated by false statements, statements which misrepresent the policies of this government.
I want to come now to a problem that concerns the province of Alberta, and concerns particularly the Bow River constituency. I refer to the coal industry. I might say that, so far as Bow River is concerned, there are two particular parts that mine coal. The first is Canmore and the second is Drum-heller. Farther south in the Macleod riding is the Crowsnest pass area. These false statements and these misrepresentations to which
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams I refer this afternoon have been made in the legislature with regard to this industry during the last five or six weeks. I believe it is my duty and my privilege as a member of parliament here to answer this new opposition who, by the way, have seen fit, because they are the critics of the federal members of parliament from Alberta, to increase their remuneration in order to compensate them for these new responsibilities.
I refer to an article published about a month ago in the Herald which says, "Get off fanny and aid coal industry". This is a criticism directed toward this particular government. I should like to refer also to a statement made in the legislature by the hon. member for Pincher Creek, to which reference is made in the press as follows:
Mr. Kovach said he has heard a lot of talk about Japan emerging as a market for Canadian coal, but so far not one ton from southern Alberta has been exported to that country.
This is the kind of misrepresentation about which I am talking. What has been the policy of this government in so far as the coal industry of western Canada is concerned, and I want to deal with western Canada because I am not one who knows the problems of Nova Scotia and the other coal mining areas in Canada. Let us just look at the record for a few minutes. When this government took office we immediately started a program of sales for coal to Japan and, in 1957, the first contract was entered into. As a result of that 40,486 tons of coal were sold. In 1958, 21,505 tons of coal were sold. In 1959, 192,857 tons of coal were sold. I am told by companies with which I have contact in Japan now that Mitsui Busan and Company Limited and Marada Steel Company are negotiating for another contract for 470,000 tons of western coal to be shipped to Japan. When you read statements made by the Hon. Gordon Taylor, minister of highways for Alberta, and other members of the legislature to the effect that there has been no coal shipped out of Alberta to Japan, and realize they are setting themselves up as critics of the federal government, then the record must be set straight. These are the people whom we must meet and with whom we must deal so far as our political future is concerned in Alberta.
Let us look at the truth about the coal industry so far as southern Alberta is concerned. What are the main criticisms they make? They say there is coal being imported into Canada from the United States. I think we will accept that. Coal was coming into Canada during the time of the Liberals, and we are prepared to say there has been coal coming in from the United States during the term of this government. Let us look at the

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams facts. There are three types of coal mined in southern Alberta. In Canmore, which is a town nestled in the Rockies on No. 1 highway between Calgary and Banff, they mine anthracite coal. This particular coal is used for coking coal, industrial coal, and that is the type of coal which Japan has been buying for its industries.
Then, the Crowsnest pass has coal. The members from Nova Scotia will know exactly what I am talking about when I say that this is a high bituminous coal. The coal in the Crowsnest pass area is on the border between British Columbia and Alberta and is the type of coal that is used in industry. It was the type of coal that was used by Canadian National and Canadian Pacific to create steam for their locomotives. This market was lost when the railways changed from steam power to diesel power. The railways, of course, did that for reasons of economics.
Then, last but not least, we come to the coal that is mined in Drumheller. The valley town of Drumheller is a good, prosperous town in that part of Alberta which is one of the best farming areas anywhere in the province. But as you drive from the town of Drumheller you drop into what might be categorized as a canyon, and there in the valley are the various coal mines that have been operating since the early 1900's. It was from these mines that the domestic fuel was obtained to keep the farm homes warm, to keep the homes warm in the villages, towns and cities of many areas. This coal is not bituminous coal, nor is it anthracite coal. This coal is sub-bituminous domestic fuel.
Let us look at these arguments. For years, the Social Credit party has been telling the coal miners and operators in Drumheller that this coal coming in from the United States is the reason the miners are out of work. By the way, for the last 15 years there has been a great problem in the Drumheller valley in so far as the coal miner keeping his shifts going in the summer months is concerned. They say that this coal is coming in from the United States, and that is the problem. Let me make myself very clear in this regard. The coal that is mined in Drumheller is not bituminous coal. The coal that comes from Pennsylvania is bituminous coal and is used in the industrial centres of Ontario. It is an entirely different type of coal from that which is mined in Drumheller. It would not matter whether one lump of coal came in from the United States or 20 million tons, it would not affect the Drumheller area because the coal that is mined in Drumheller is a domestic fuel which has been used for that purpose for the past 60 years, the Drumheller coal could not and cannot be used in this class of industry.

Something new has appeared on the horizon in Canada. Our newspapers are full of it now. I refer to the competition between fuels such as oil and natural gas. Mr. Manning who heads that party and is prime minister of Alberta honestly admits that the reason there is a labour problem in the Drumheller valley is the competition of oil, propane and natural gas. Today when we go on farms in western Canada, the same as in eastern Canada, we find that these homes are heated in the winter by oil or propane. We need only to go to places like Calgary, Edmonton and other urban centres in Alberta or places in Saskatchewan or Manitoba in order to find that natural gas which is clean and convenient is the new domestic fuel.
It is because of the development of the petroleum industry in Alberta-and I am one who stands in my place and endorses it- that the onus by the provincial government has been put on the coal operators and these men have been put out of work who live in Wayne, East Coulee and other places, to which I could take you this afternoon. While the Social Credit party have wanted to take credit for the development of the petroleum industry, they will not take the blame for the adversity of the coal industry. There we have the inconsistency. There we have the misrepresentation. There we have the false position in which they stand today as far as this industry is concerned.
I might say that when you read on in this article you find that Hon. Gordon Taylor minister of highways, places the full onus of the problem of unemployment in the Drumheller valley on the federal government, he places it not only on this government but on the Liberal government. Surely a province that has received $1 billion from the petroleum and natural gas industry, and which by the development of this industry has seen this change-over from the energy of coal to the energy of petroleum, has some responsibility to these people in the province of Alberta who are unemployed owing to that new industry.
Last but not least, the province of Alberta, since the Social Credit party took over has received millions of dollars in royalties from the coal industry but not one of those dollars has been put back into the industry either to help the operators or the coal miners. That is the reason why I brought in provincial politics this afternoon. They are playing federal politics and I suggest it is up to members of parliament from Alberta to answer these misrepresentations concerning the coal industry and other industries about which they care to speak in their legislature. The Social Credit government instead of giving the facts actually preach falsehoods.

I should like to direct the remainder of my remarks to the natural gas industry of Alberta. The recent announcement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce approving the decision of the energy board in granting licences to four companies, namely Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited; Alberta and Southern Gas Company; Canadian-Montana Pipe Line Company and Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, to export natural gas from western Canada will mean three real benefits economically to this country. First, it will create an industrial expansion in Alberta and the rest of Canada beyond the vision of the greatest visionary. Second, it will assist Canada in correcting its unbalanced and unfavourable trade with the United States. Third, it will create top flight jobs for Canadians and full employment in the province of Alberta and in other parts of western Canada.
We have heard from the Liberal party some criticism in this chamber of late of the delay in the export of gas. I should like to answer that criticism this afternoon. But before doing so I should like to refer to an article which appeared in Saturday Night of February 6, 1960. It was written by Edwin Copps and it was headed "The Energetic Energy Board". This is what he said:
If all its performances are as good as its premiere-
He was speaking of the board.
-the national energy board may stand as one of the Diefenbaker government's best acomplish-ments to date. At its first public hearing in Ottawa this month, the new five-man board put on a show of efficiency and expertness-
In brief he said that of all the things we have accomplished this one may go down as the greatest of the Diefenbaker government. What does he say about the situation if these licences to export gas were approved and as to what it would mean? I am going to deal with that matter in a few moments but first I want to read further from the same article at page 22 of the magazine:
If all these permits are granted, the revenue to Canada from the gas sales alone will be upwards of $170 million a year. The resulting expansion in Canada's natural gas industry will create some 40,000 new jobs, yield a livelihood for some 200,000 Canadian citizens. It will trigger a $500 million program of new industrial development in the country-pipe lines, gathering systems, processing plants and all the other elaborate installations the natural gas industry needs.
What a contrast that is to what the hon. member for Assiniboia had to say. In one breath he speaks about unemployment and in the next breath he is opposed to the export of gas. This article states that the resulting expansion will create 40,000 new jobs in Alberta, will create 200,000 new jobs throughout Canada and will bring each year
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams $170 million into Canada from the United States in order to help, as I said previously, to balance our unfavourable trade relations with that country. I say this personally; I have said it outside of this house and I say it here today. I think this will be the greatest boon for western Canada since the early days when agriculture began to boom in the early 1900's.
What has been our stand in this regard? The Liberals have accused us of delay. Let us see where the Liberal party stood in the province of Alberta. Since 1951-and I can speak with some authority in this regard- the provincial Liberal leader at that time, namely Mr. Prowse-he gave up the leadership in 1957 to Mr. Grant McEwan-was opposed to any export of gas in Alberta. Mr. Grant McEwan, speaking in the Bow River riding during the provincial election in 1958 and in the Thorncliffe area in the city of Calgary made the definite statement that he too was opposed to the export of natural gas from Alberta to the United States. Both these leaders have stood out against the export of natural gas from the province of Alberta. How can the Liberal party here in the opposition say that we are responsible for the delay when their party took the stand in western Canada that they were against any export whatsoever? We also have the record of another member of their party, a senior member of the legislature for many years. I refer to Mr. Hugh John MacDonald. He is still against the export of gas.
What has been this government's stand? When this government took office-and I have said this previously but I should like to repeat it-this government set up the Borden commission. Why was the Borden commission set up? It was set up so that the facts would be obtained and determined with regard to how much natural gas we have for the foreseeable future needs of Canada and how much surplus we have to export. What was their report in that regard? Their report was quite simple. They said there were proven reserves in the province of Alberta of 23.7 trillion cubic feet and an estimated reserve of 300 trillion cubic feet. Then when the energy board was set up they revised the figures and said there are actually proven reserves of 30.5 trillion cubic feet. Those figures do not mean much unless you take a look at what Canada needs for its foreseeable future requirements.
Before I read these figures out, let me just say something more about the board. How can you ever come to a decision or how can the energy board ever come to a decision without the proper facts before them? How

The Budget-Mr. Woolliams can a judge come to a decision when he is judging a case unless he has the evidence before him? Hence the energy board was set up. This energy board should have been set up five years ago or ten years ago. These facts should have been before the proper department so that the export of gas could have gone forward two, three of four years ago from the province of Alberta because the figures now show that we had necessary surplus reserves.
To come back to the question of what are Canada's needs in the foreseeable future, keeping in mind the fact that we have in the province of Alberta proven reserves of 30 trillion cubic feet, may I say this? We will use in 1960 an estimated amount of natural gas of 344.15 billion cubic feet, and by 1989 we will need 1,608.63 billion cubic feet. If you add up all our needs from 1960 to 1989 you will find we will need approximately 29,765 billion cubic feet, which is approximately 30 trillion cubic feet.
In other words, we have proven reserves in Alberta for the needs of Canada for the next 30 years. That was stated in the report of the energy board. Even at a conservative estimate, if we find 2.5 trillion cubic feet of gas each year by normal exploration-this is set out in both the Borden report and the energy board report-we will probably have to drill between 360 to 400 new wells a year. It is estimated that by 1989 we will have in this country proven reserves of 92 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. So not only can we take care of our foreseeable needs in the future of Canada but we can take care of those export commitments and have a reserve of some 40 trillion cubic feet at the end of that time.
Therefore I say without any reservation, and I have taken this stand in the house and outside, that I am in favour and always have been of exporting natural gas from western Canada. Today we have the proof and I want to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) for recommending and approving on behalf of this government the export of gas to the United States.
Now I want to answer some criticisms offered to this government by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) when he talked about millionaires. I take this position. Since when was it a sin to make a dollar out of farming? Since when was it a sin to make a dollar out of natural gas? Since when was it a sin to make a dollar out of any business? The labourer has come a long way since the day I dug manholes in the streets of Moose Jaw in 1938 to work myself through university. Labour realizes today that when business makes a dollar, they, too,

can make a dollar and their standard of living goes up accordingly. How can labour earn higher wages if the industry which employs them is insolvent? That is something which I feel is a lesson that the leader of the C.C.F. party would do well to learn. I repeat; when business does well, so does the labourer because, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said today, we in Canada have the highest standard of living in the world.
Now I come to one last point, and that is the reference to some criticism which has been offered of our leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). During this session in particular there have been some personal attacks made against him. Often they referred to his statement that as long as he was Prime Minister of Canada he would see no man or woman would suffer. I think it depends on what definition you put on the word "suffer". I think in my day when I was unemployed as a young man if I could have enjoyed unemployment insurance I would not have suffered. But I do know this, and I know everyone will agree with me, that there is no place in the world where we have a greater opportunity than right here in Canada.
When I was in Japan I listened to their problems, and when I told them of our problems they laughed. I said our problem is that we have too much butter, that we have too much beef, that we have too much wheat, too much uranium, too much natural gas and too much petroleum. What a problem. But what an opportunity for 18 million people if those people today will go out and work-and I think they will because I have confidence in Canadians -with the same vision of the pioneers who developed this country. I think that is the type of vision that our leader the Prime Minister has in reference to Canada.
I learned my lesson well when I listened to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). He said the members of parliament should take home a bag of books every night. So I started taking home a bag of books every night, and by good fortune I picked up an article written on January 21, 1947 about a distinguished member of parliament, and at that time he himself was just an ordinary M.P. This is what this writer had to say. He is a distinguished writer for the Ottawa Citizen, Austin F. Cross, who was writing in "Western Business and Industry", volume 21, January 1947, page 54. He wrote:
John Diefenbaker is no ordinary member but a national figure. It was he who was making himself heard in the councils of the great, it was the member for Lake Centre putting Lake Centre on the map. That's why this Saskatchewan riding returned him by the astounding majority of 1,009 on June

11, 1945. With every other Progressive Conservative candidate in Saskatchewan beaten, even with the Liberals ending up with a mere two members of parliament, John Diefenbaker came through as easily as if the had been running in Toronto.
Last but not least he says this:
What about tomorrow?
He was talking about his characteristics.
I'd say that John could go as far as they want him to go. In parliamentary debate he is as good as the best, most of the time. Buttressed by the authority that being in the government lends you he would make a superb cabinet minister. He could fill any one of half a dozen portfolios with distinction. If, by the long arm of circumstance-
This is certainly looking into the future.
-he some day was given the party leadership, he could make not only a great but inspired prime minister.
Nothing that needs ability, nothing that calls for ambition, nothing that demands enterprise, would stop John Diefenbaker on his climb to the top. All he wants is the call. When or if it comes, John's ready.
I would say to those critics who personally attack our Prime Minister that I, as a man of western Canada who has seen the development of his character, am confident as I stand in my place that I speak for every member on the back benches, and I am sure they have full confidence in the leader of this party and the Prime Minister of this country.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to associate myself with those who, this afternoon, offered their condolences to the Liberal opposition whip in this house, (Mr. Habel) on the death of his wife. I wish to tender him my deeply felt sympathy in his cruel bereavement.
Mr. Speaker, during the few remaining minutes before adjournment, I propose to speak of the budget, but in another way than is usually heard in this house.
First of all, I must commend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) for the brilliant manner in which he outlined the situation, in reply to the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). He put his finger right on the problems now facing the Canadian public, contrary to the Minister of Finance who, wearing a wide grin, complacently stated in this house that everything was for the best under Conservative rule.
Mr. Speaker, I want briefly to point out to hon. members that everything is not as perfect as the Minister of Finance said it was. As a matter of fact, I wonder whether the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis (Mr. Diefenbaker) and all the friends of the Conservative party who are in this house, do not feel a bit awkward when rising before the Canadian people to say that all goes well, when everyone in Canada knows that we have now over 800,000 unemployed in this country. How could they help being embarrassed, especially after the Conservative leader formally promised throughout this country that "if he was returned to power, no one would suffer in Canada".
Mr. Speaker, there are people who suffer in Canada, but the Prime Minister offers no excuse for not keeping his promises. Furthermore, there was the other promise to the effect that the day after the elections he was to launch "a famous billion dollar public works program". We are still looking for the projects that would come out of that promise. A tax reduction had also been promised as soon as the Conservatives returned to power. We have had tax increases instead. The end of budget surpluses had also been promised, since taxes would be lowered. That promise, Mr. Speaker, has indeed been kept because instead of surpluses we have had deplorable deficits, three of them in a row, since our friends opposite were returned to power.
And, today Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance, all smiles, is announcing that he foresees a $12 million surplus for the coming fiscal year. Well, this prospect of a $12 million surplus, take it with a grain of salt, because we recall the promises made by the Conservative party during election time, and which were never kept at any time or in any way.
The Prime Minister had promised to find new markets all over the world for our manufactured products. Has he found any? Not at all, Mr. Speaker. We are now faced with an export deficit, the volume of our exports being lower than that of our imports.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance said all sorts of things, but this is precisely what he forgot to tell us the other evening in his budget speech. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to go back over the record of the last two years and mention some points which the minister has omitted.
On the day of the Minister of Finance's speech, two years had elapsed since the Conservative party was elected to office, and on the occasion of that second anniversary, it is fitting to recall what our dear Conservative friends have given us since they took over this great country.
2980	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
First, I should recall the C.B.C. strike, which was settled after unbelievable delays on the part of the government, not to mention the part played by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) who practised an ostrich policy and stuck his head in the sand to avoid looking at the problems. There is also that famous matter of winter navigation which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) had promised. As for agriculture, it is completely depressed. There is also the notorious feud between members of the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada. Then there was the fight over the "tight money policy", which was also covered by a definite promise by the Prime Minister who had declared that if he was returned to power he would do away with the tight money policy. Yet money was never so scarce as it has been since the Conservatives were returned to power.
Mr. Speaker, there is a deficit in exports, and a slow down in house building, where the situation is getting worse. Everything is known. We read it in the papers: there will be less house building this year than ever before.
While we are discussing problems of much interest, we, from the province of Quebec, note that the ministers from the province of Quebec never take part in the discussion, and merely keep silent when mention is made of problems of such importance as federal-provincial relations, the trans-Canada highway and unemployment.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is a shame to see ministers remain in their seats and make no effort to take a stand in such important circumstances.
When the government is reminded of unemployment, the depression, the tight money policy, the conflict with the governor of the Bank of Canada, the confusion in national defence, the mess in agriculture, our friends opposite reply: "You are prophets of doom and gloom, you have no confidence in your country, you see nothing but blue ruin."
Mr. Speaker, I would very much like to be able to sing praises about the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance. I would like, as would all Canadian citizens, to be able to rejoice over the achiements of a Tory government. But like everyone else, I cannot help facing the fact and, in the face of those facts, I cannot help blaming the Conservative government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I wish first to join with those hon. members of the house who have expressed condolences to the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel), the whip of the official opposition party, in his bereavement.
I should also like to add my words to those of previous participants in this debate in complimenting our Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on bringing in a balanced budget designed for these troubled times and one that has been balanced without an increase in taxes. Despite this fact taxes are still lower than when the previous government was in power.
In the time at my disposal I should like to bring to the attention of the house some questions of vital concern not only to my constituency of St. John's East but also of concern to the constituencies of my genial and learned colleague the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's (Mr. Batten), the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Granger) and the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) because in each of these constituencies there is located United States defence installations employing many thousands of Canadian citizens.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on April 15, 1959, replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), stated that as of March 31, 1959 there were 4,324 Canadian citizens employed on United States bases in Newfoundland and Newfoundland-Labrador. This is a matter of interest and concern, as I said before, not only to my own constituency but to the constituencies of other hon. members in this house.
In my own riding of St. John's East there is located on the shores of Quidi Vidi lake a beautiful white city which was originally known as Fort Pepperrell and in later years as Pepperrell air force base. This is one of the four bases given to the United States by the United Kingdom in the early war years but not necessarily as part of the famous destroyers for bases deal, that deal in which the United Kingdom in our hour of need leased military bases to the United States government in return for 50 destroyers. On the contrary, bases in Newfoundland-Labrador and I believe those military installations in the colony of Bermuda were leased to the United States government on a gratis basis; there was no quid pro quo. I cannot speak with authority for the colony of Bermuda but I feel I can speak for the then colony of Newfoundland, which is now part of

Canada. Newfoundland at that time had no elected government. Our constitution was suspended in 1933 because of a financial crisis in the then world-wide economic depression.
These bases were assigned to the United States government at various strategic locations in Newfoundland and in Newfound-land-Labrador territory on a 99-year lease basis. At that time nobody was in a position to argue and present the case of the government and the people of Newfoundland; for ours at that time was a colonial administration, governed directly by Westminster.
The folly of this course of action is now coming home to us. With the great changes in North American defence, the advent of the atomic age, the advent of the ballistic missile, no longer is it necessary for world powers to maintain fighter bases, not to mention bases strictly of a military nature. Pepperrell air force base was one of those bases which was leased in 1940. The people in Newfoundland had no say in the matter. They had no choice, no voice in their sovereign territory being leased to another power, yet a friendly power, for a period of 99 years without a dollar in exchange. Mind you, were I to say that those bases, those United States defence installations, were not a boon to our country and our province now would be to distort the facts, because I would say without qualification that United States defence spending in Newfoundland and Labrador, as an economic factor in our progress, ranks on an equal basis with the economic impact of confederation in 1949.
As I said a few minutes ago, the folly of the action in 1940 of the then imperial government could have had very serious and very tragic human consequences to the many thousands of Canadian citizens now employed on those bases. One thing can be said,
The Budget-Mr. McGrath namely that it was a very insecure position; nevertheless the fact remains that those people who did accept employment in 1941 did so with the realization that the bases were to remain for 99 years; consequently, it was logical for them to assume that their employment would be of a permanent nature.
Yet, it was not until a few years ago that those four or five thousand Canadian citizens were even enjoying the benefits of unemployment insurance. It was only a few days ago that it was announced in St. John's and in this house that the long fight those people have waged to be recognized as pensionable employees of the United States government in Canada has finally borne fruit. This is of prime importance to my constituents because it has been announced that the United States air force base in St. John's, beautiful Fort Pepperrell, on the shores of Quidi Vidi, is about to terminate its operations. It is with a little nostalgia, it is with a saddened heart, that we say goodbye to those friends whom we have cultivated over the past two decades. I am pleased to say they are leaving under good auspices, because, through the good offices of the United States government, in consultation with the government of Canada, the rights of those Canadian citizens to a pension, which is the least price that can be paid, has been recognized.
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
